title: Diamond Star Pattern
description: Brute force to optimized: per-cell space-or-star checks versus measuring each row by its distance from the nearest tip and building it directly, then batching the whole pattern into one output call.

blocks.text: Given a positive integer n, print a solid diamond made of stars with 2n minus 1 rows, widening from a single star at the top down to a widest row of 2n minus 1 stars in the middle, then narrowing back down to a single star at the bottom.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Pyramid Stacked on Its Own Reflection
blocks.text: A diamond is simply the centered pyramid seen earlier, stacked directly on top of its own upside down reflection, with the widest row shared between the two halves. Distance from either the very top tip or the very bottom tip determines exactly how wide that row needs to be.

blocks.caption: Each row widens toward the middle, then narrows again toward the bottom tip

blocks.content: {"headers":["Row","Output","Why"],"rows":[["Row 1","   *","Distance from the nearest tip, m, is 1, since row 1 is 1 step from the top tip, giving 2m minus 1 equal to 1 star."],["Row 2","  ***","m is 2, one step further from the top tip, giving 3 stars."],["Row 3"," *****","m is 3, still widening toward the middle."],["Row 4","*******","m is 4, the widest row, exactly midway between both tips."],["Row 5"," *****","m is 3 again, now measured from the bottom tip instead of the top, since row 5 is 3 steps from row 7."],["Row 6","  ***","m is 2, narrowing toward the bottom tip."],["Row 7","   *","m is 1, the final row, a single step from the bottom tip."]]}

blocks.text: With n = 1, both tips collapse into the same single row, a single star.
No rows at all, so nothing is printed.

The most tempting first approach is to write one loop for the widening top half and a second loop for the narrowing bottom half. It is worth pausing to ask whether both halves can actually share a single formula.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A diamond is symmetric about its middle row, so the top half and the bottom half are mirror images of each other, both governed by the exact same odd, growing-then-shrinking star count.

Observation 2: Rather than tracking which half a row belongs to, each row can instead be measured by a single number, its distance from whichever tip, top or bottom, happens to be nearer.

Observation 3: Testing this against a small example, n equal to 4, confirms it: row 3 and row 5 are both distance 3 from their nearer tip and produce the exact same star count, even though one is in the top half and the other is in the bottom half.

Observation 4: Once that single distance value is known for row r, the exact same gap-and-odd-star-count formula already derived for the full pyramid applies directly, with no separate logic needed for which half the row is in.
That reframing, measuring distance from the nearer tip instead of tracking which half a row is in, is what collapses two separate loops into one shared formula.

For every row, first work out how far that row is from the nearer of the two tips, then use two nested loops, printing a single space or star one character at a time based on the leading gap for that row.

items: Loop over every row r, from 1 to 2n minus 1.
Compute m, the distance of this row from whichever tip is closer, top or bottom.
Compute the gap, n minus m, and the star count, 2m minus 1.
Check every column, printing a space while still in the gap, and a star afterward.
After finishing a row, move to the next line.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: find the distance from the nearest tip, then print space or star per column

codes.python:
def diamond_pattern(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):          # r counts every row, top tip to bottom tip
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)                     # this row's distance from the nearest tip
        gap = n - m
        stars = 2 * m - 1
        for j in range(gap + stars):               # check every column this row actually uses
            if j < gap:
                print(" ", end="")                    # still inside the leading gap
            else:
                print("*", end="")                    # inside the star region
        print()                                    # move to the next line after the row


if __name__ == "__main__":
    diamond_pattern(4)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: m is computed once per row as the minimum of r and 2n minus r, capturing in a single number whether this row is still widening toward the middle or already narrowing toward the bottom tip.

gap and stars are derived from m using the exact same formulas as the plain full pyramid, n minus m and 2m minus 1, so the shape of each individual row still needs no special casing for which half it belongs to.
The inner loop still checks each column one at a time, printing a single character per iteration, which is exactly the inefficiency the optimized version removes.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every row correctly measures its distance from the nearer tip, and every column within that row is checked individually against the resulting gap.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since the total stars across the full diamond is proportional to n squared, and every position is checked one at a time.
Space: O(1) extra space, no string is ever built.

Limitation: once the gap and star count for a row are known, checking every column individually adds nothing, both regions can be built directly in a single operation each, exactly as with the plain centered pyramid earlier.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why checking every column works but is wasteful: once m is already known for a row, printing its gap and star region one character at a time repeats a decision that a single direct construction could make in one step.

What stays the same as the full pyramid: the underlying formula, n minus m spaces and 2m minus 1 stars, is identical, only the meaning of the row number has changed from i to a distance-from-nearest-tip value m.

What is genuinely new here: a single formula now covers both the widening top half and the narrowing bottom half, because m already folds both directions into one number.

Can the same direct-construction technique be reused unchanged: yes, exactly as with the full pyramid, a repeat operation builds the gap and another builds the star region, regardless of which half the row is measured from.

The core idea: compute m once per row, then build the gap and star region directly from it, exactly as with a plain full pyramid.

For each row, compute its distance from the nearer tip once, then build the leading gap and the star region directly, using one operation each, and concatenate them into a single row string. This removes all per cell branching, needing only one print call per row.
For each row, compute its distance from the nearer tip once, then build the gap and the star region directly and print the whole row with a single call.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: find the distance from the nearest tip, build the row directly

codes.python:
def diamond_pattern(n):
    total_rows = 2 * n - 1
    for r in range(1, total_rows + 1):          # r counts every row, top tip to bottom tip
        m = min(r, 2 * n - r)                     # this row's distance from the nearest tip
        row = " " * (n - m) + "*" * (2 * m - 1)     # build spaces and stars directly, no per cell checks
        print(row)                               # one print call per row instead of per character


if __name__ == "__main__":
    diamond_pattern(4)

blocks.text: This works because m, the minimum of r and 2n minus r, correctly measures every row's distance from whichever tip is nearer, so the same n minus m spaces and 2m minus 1 stars formula from the full pyramid applies uniformly across the entire diamond; a direct repeat operation still constructs each region in one step, with no dependence on tracking which half a row belongs to. As r increases from 1 to n, m grows from 1 to n; as r continues past n up to 2n minus 1, m shrinks back down from n minus 1 to 1, producing the correct widen-then-narrow shape automatically.

items: m is computed once per row as the minimum of r and 2n minus r, the single value that captures both which half the row is in and how far it is from that half's tip.
A direct repeat operation builds the n minus m space gap, and another builds the 2m minus 1 star region, exactly the same construction technique already used for the plain full pyramid.
Concatenating those two pieces and printing once per row completes the entire diamond without ever writing separate logic for the top half versus the bottom half.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) total characters produced, the same as the brute force, but with no per cell branching and only O(n) print calls instead of O(n squared) checks.
Space: O(n), for the single row string being built and printed at a time.
10. Further Optimization: A Single Output Call

Every row is already being built directly in one operation, so instead of printing each one separately, all rows can be built first, joined together with newline characters, and the entire pattern can be produced with a single output call.

blocks.caption: Further optimization: join every row into one string and output it in a single call

items: Every row is still built directly from its own m value, exactly as in the optimized version, the only change is collecting each finished row instead of printing it immediately.
Joining all 2n minus 1 rows with newline characters assembles the complete diamond as a single string, entirely in memory, before any output call happens.
A single print call at the very end outputs the whole diamond, cutting the operation count down to exactly 1 regardless of how large n is.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), the same total characters produced.
Space: O(n squared), to hold every row joined into one string before the single output call. This trades some memory for the fewest possible output calls, exactly one, no matter how large n is.

blocks.text: A diamond is simply two centered pyramids joined at their widest row, and measuring a row by its distance from the nearer tip lets the exact same gap and star count formula from a plain pyramid be reused for the entire shape, without treating the top and bottom halves as separate cases.

items: Printing the widest row twice, once for the bottom of the top half and again for the top of the bottom half, instead of sharing it once.
Using the row index directly instead of its distance from the nearer tip, which breaks the narrowing bottom half.
Forgetting the n = 0 edge case, where nothing at all should be printed.

blocks.text: Framing a diamond as a distance from the nearest tip, rather than as two separate loops for a top half and a bottom half, is a cleaner mental model that avoids duplicating the row formula and the risk of getting the two halves slightly out of sync.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can this be one loop instead of two", think: measure each row's distance from the nearer tip, min of r and 2n minus r, and reuse a single formula.
If the interviewer says "how is this related to the full pyramid", think: it is the same gap and odd star count formula, just fed a distance-from-nearest-tip value instead of the row index directly.
If the interviewer says "can you reduce this to one output call", think: build every row first, join with newlines, print once.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: All three versions produce the same O(n squared) total characters, since that is fixed by the shape itself. What changes is how that output is organized: per cell checks in the brute force version, one formula built row per print call in the optimized version, and exactly one call for the entire pattern in the further optimized version.

items: Pattern: pattern printing where a shape symmetric about its middle row is measured by distance from the nearer tip, reusing a single formula for both the widening and narrowing halves instead of writing two separate loops.

Core Idea: compute m, a row's distance from whichever tip is nearer, as min of r and 2n minus r, then reuse the full pyramid's n minus m spaces and 2m minus 1 stars formula directly, with no special casing for which half the row is in.
Time: O(n squared) checks for the brute force, O(n) output calls for the optimized version, O(1) for the further optimized version; total characters printed are always O(n squared).
Space: O(1) extra for the brute force, O(n) for the current row, O(n squared) for the fully joined pattern.
Most Important Observation: a shape that looks symmetric about a middle point can often be described by a single distance-based formula instead of two separate halves.
Interview Difficulty: easy to produce the correct shape with two loops; collapsing both halves into one distance measurement is what shows real pattern recognition.
One line memory trick: m equals min of r and 2n minus r, then reuse the full pyramid's formula on m.
